Scenarios

Adaptation to Climate Change, supplied daily climate pro-

sidered 47 projections, including 30 Coupled Model

soil. We acknowledge that replacing impervious surfaces
with wetlands could have led to greater impacts (and the
identiﬁcation of lower restoration targets), but we decided to
test scenarios that would be easier for decision-makers to
envision (due to the high socio-economic cost of imper-
vious surface removal). For each restoration scenario, we
ran the model for the entire period from 1979 to 2099. In
each run, the ﬁrst year was used as a spin-up period. Daily
stream ﬂows were simulated at each sub-watershed outlet.
The 1980–2019 time period was deﬁned as the reference
period, when comparing to future temporal horizons. Model
calibration parameters were not modiﬁed for climate change
simulations.
Analyses of River Flow Changes Under Future
Climate and Restoration Scenarios
We assessed the effect that projected climate change and
wetland restoration scenarios would have on spring peak
ﬂow and low summer ﬂow at sub-watershed outlets (a.k.a.,
hydroclimatic assessment). Spring peak ﬂows were identi-
ﬁed as those occurring within the March-April-May period,
and summer low ﬂows within the July-August-September
period. For spring peak ﬂows, we used the 2-year (Q2) and
20-year (Q20) daily maximum ﬂow indicators, and for
summer low ﬂows the 2-year (Q2-7) and 10-year (Q10-7)
minimum average ﬂows over seven consecutive days. As a
ﬁrst step, we illustrated the effect of climate change on daily
ﬂow regimes and ﬂow indicators using hydrographs and
boxplots, respectively, and compared them to the reference
period (i.e., under current wetland conditions). Daily ﬂow
data were log-transformed and standardized (mean of 0 and
standard deviation of 1) per sub-watershed to facilitate
comparison of ﬂow dynamics among sub-watersheds. Flow
indicators were standardized per sub-watershed, as well as
per ﬂow indicator, to focus on temporal trends speciﬁc to
each indicator separately. We then illustrated how different
wetland restoration scenarios made it possible to mitigate
the effects of climate change on ﬂow indicators using
density plots.
To quantify the difference in ﬂow indicators between the
reference period and a given scenario (hereafter referred to
as the ﬂow change), we considered the whole set of indi-
cator values obtained from the 47 climate projections (47
values per scenario). Hence, for each indicator, we calcu-
lated the pairwise ﬂow differences, where all values of the
reference period were subtracted from all values of a given
scenario (leading to 47 2 = 2209 paired differences). This
approach makes it possible to account for the whole dis-
tribution of values obtained from the 47 climate projections
considered in each scenario instead of comparing means or
medians (Rousselet et al. 2017). We then reported the
median value
of these
pairwise
differences
and the
conﬁdence intervals around the median at alpha = 0.95,
calculated by bootstrapping, using the function two.boot of
the simpleboot R package (Peng 2008; R Core Team 2020).
This approach made it possible to mathematically iden-
tify the levels of restoration needed to "fully compensate"
for the climate change effects on critical ﬂows (ﬂow
change = 0). Because the precise level of restoration may
occur at a mid-point between scenarios (20, 50, 100, and
150% increase of wetland area), we conducted a linear
interpolation of ﬂow changes. This enabled identiﬁcation of
the "exact" restoration target for each indicator and horizon
where the ﬂow change would reach zero, and thus where
wetland restoration ‘completely’ compensates for climate
change effects on peak- and low-ﬂows.
Results
Climate Change Effects on Hydrology
Our results show that, under our tested scenarios, all sub-
watersheds
experience
increased
future
daily
ﬂows
throughout the winter, and an earlier snowmelt in the spring
(Fig. 2). Average daily winter ﬂows (December-January-
February) at the horizon 2020–2059 are 3.5% higher than in
the reference period, and 4.2% higher at the horizon
2060–2099 across all sub-watersheds and climatic projec-
tions. The highest increase occurs in the Jaune sub-
watershed (9%). The latter is the only sub-watershed
showing a substantial increase in spring peak ﬂows, with
mean values, for both horizons, showing an increase of 16%
for Q2, and 28% for Q20 (t-test, p < 0.01). In general, the
other sub-watersheds display only marginal changes in
these mean peak ﬂow indicators (variation of ±6%;
p < 0.05). Exceptions are the Nelson, showing a signiﬁcant
reduction of 15% for Q2 and 26% for Q20 (average for both
horizons), as well as the St. Charles, with a 14% reduction
for Q2 by 2060–2099. In the case of summer drought
events, all sub-watersheds show more severe low ﬂows in
the future, with highly similar trends of ~10% reduction in
both low ﬂow indicators by 2020–2059, and ~25% reduc-
tion by 2060–2099 (p < 0.05).
Compensation for Climate Change Effects
Figure 3 offers a visual representation of how restoration
can mitigate the effects of climate change on peak and low
ﬂows. Since the Jaune sub-watershed undergoes signiﬁcant
increases in the severity of both peak and low ﬂows in the
future, it is shown here to illustrate the impact of restoration
(here, for Q2 and Q2-7 indicators; but see Fig. S2 for Q20
and Q10-7). The results indicate that the restoration scenario

We used the following physiographic datasets to prepare
the integration of the St. Charles watershed in the PHYSI-
TEL/HYDROTEL modeling platform: (i) a ﬁve-meter
resolution digital elevation model (DEM) derived from a
Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) survey provided by
Quebec City municipal authorities; (ii) a vectorial hydro-
graphic network that includes a simpliﬁed mapping of the
urban drainage system (modeled as open channel) in the
southern (downstream) and most urbanized portion of the
watershed (Scarpari Spolidorio 2019); (iii) a land cover
representation of the watershed in 2014 (Blanchette et al.
2019), and (iv) a soil type map including nine soil texture
classes
elaborated
from
geomorphological
and
topo-
graphical data (Audet et al. 1997; Scarpari Spolidorio
2019). To process the input datasets, PHYSITEL uses
topographic and hydrographic data to discretize the water-
shed
into
relatively
homogeneous
hydrological
units
(RHHUs; Table S1), hereafter referred to as hillslopes. This
discretization of the watershed differs from the concept of
hydrological response units (HRUs), in which the sub-
watershed is subdivided into sub-basins, and then into
HRUs that possess a unique combination of land cover, land
management and soils (Neitsch et al. 2002; Dehotin and
Braud 2008). In PHYSITEL, the discretization into hill-
slopes is based on surface ﬂow directions derived from the
DEM and the D8-LTD algorithm (Orlandini et al. 2003) and
the discretized river network, leading to three hillslopes for
headwater river segments and two hillslopes for all other
river segments (Rousseau et al. 2011; Fossey et al. 2015).
Next, PHYSITEL identiﬁes wetlands using the land cover
data, and categorizes them as either isolated or riparian
wetlands based on a user-deﬁned adjacency threshold,
referring to the percentage of pixels in direct contact with
the hydrographic network (1%). Then, PHYSITEL deline-
ates the contributing area of each wetland by processing the
ﬂow direction/accumulation matrix. Finally, since both
wetland modules in HYDROTEL rely on the hydrologically
equivalent wetland (HEW) concept (Wang et al. 2008),
PHYSITEL aggregates wetlands into one isolated HEW
and/or riparian HEW per hillslope.
HYDROTEL is built around eight computational mod-
ules, each offering different algorithms to simulate the
distinct components of the hydrological cycle: meteor-
ological data interpolation, snowpack accumulation and
melting,
soil
temperature
and
frost,
potential
evapo-
transpiration, vertical water balance, surface runoff routing,
river ﬂow routing, and wetland (isolated and riparian)
hydrology. In this project, the empirically based equation
developed by Hydro-Quebec (Dionne et al. 2008; Isabelle
2014) was selected to quantify the potential evapo-
transpiration at hillslope scale among the seven equations
integrated in the model. The efﬁciency and simplicity of this
method, which relies solely on daily maximum and
minimum temperatures, explains its frequent use in hydro-
logical modeling applications in the province of Quebec.
Additionally, as described by Fossey et al. (2015), the two
wetland modules in the modeling platform provide a means
of explicitly simulating isolated wetlands (IWs) and riparian
wetlands (RWs). Golden et al. (2014) described IWs geo-
graphically as "depressional wetlands that are completely
surrounded by uplands". Consequently, IWs are not expli-
citly connected to the river network via surface ﬂow paths,
although overﬂow can occur. With their direct connection to
the river network, riparian wetlands are inﬂuenced by the
ﬂow of the adjacent river segment, and thus the model
accounts for ﬂow exchange between them (Liu et al. 2008).
These differences also induce a spatial variability in the
hydrological services provided by wetlands, with, as
reported in recent studies, a greater contribution of isolated
wetlands in regulating stream ﬂows when located upstream
rather than downstream, and a greater contribution of
riparian wetlands when located downstream (Fossey et al.
2016). Both wetland modules are integrated at the RHHU
level and conceptualized as a control volume in the vertical
water balance. The results of the isolated wetland module
are transferred to the surface runoff routing module, while
those of the riparian wetland module are partially integrated
into the vertical water balance with a direct link to the river
ﬂow routing module. Equations (1) and (2) describe the
hydrological budgets of both isolated and riparian wetlands,
respectively (all terms are expressed in m3):
Vwet2 ¼ Vwet1 þ Vpcp  Vev  Vseep  Vfout þ Vfin
ð1Þ
Vwet2 ¼ Vwet1 þ Vpcp  Vev  Vseep  Vex þ Vfin
ð2Þ
where Vwet2 and Vwet1 are the volume of water stored in the
HEW at the end and at the beginning of each time step,
respectively, Vpcp is the volume of precipitation falling on
the HEW, Vev is the volume of water lost to evapotranspira-
tion estimated as a fraction (nominal value = 0.6) of the
evapotranspiration at the RHHU scale, Vseep is the volume
of water transferred to a deep aquifer (but forwarded to river
ﬂow because the model does not allow any water loss), Vfout
is the outﬂow from the HEW, Vex is the volume of water
exchanged with the river segment, and Vﬁn is the volume of
water entering the HEW. For a complete description of the
wetland modules and equations, the reader should refer to
Fossey et al. (2015).
For model calibration, we assembled a meteorological
dataset of daily precipitation, minimum and maximum
temperatures recorded by Environment and Climate Change
Canada (63 meteorological stations) and Quebec City (31
rain gauges) covering the 1969–2020 period. We performed
the model calibration using the Optimization Software
Toolkit for Research Involving Computational Heuristics

parameters and set the least sensitive parameters of the
model (Table S2) based on previous knowledge and recent
sensitivity analyses. The values of the wetland parameters
were assigned accounting for the dominant typology (eg.:
swamp, fen, bog, marsh, etc.) at HEW scale, based on the
knowledge of the ﬁeld experts consulted (Table S2). Using
a daily time-step, we calibrated each sub-watershed inde-
pendently, except for the St. Charles watershed, where the
calibrated parameters of the Hurons, Nelson and Jaune
Rivers were applied. We performed ten trials of 250 itera-
tions for each sub-watershed, running the model for the
period corresponding to hydrometric
data availability
(Table 1), and removing the ﬁrst simulated year to minimize
model initialization errors. Also, when assessing model
calibration, the objective function did not use November-to-
March stream ﬂows from the simulated data to avoid
accounting for the uncertainty associated to ice-covered
measurements (Chokmani et al. 2008). As recommended by
Shen et al. (2022), the use of the longest and most recent
available period of data was preferred to the split-sample
calibration strategy, as the former increases robustness.
Simulated data were compared with observed data derived
from a network of hydrometric stations within the St.
Charles River watershed (MELCC 2021). The ﬁnal para-
meter set was selected among the best solutions of each trial
as the best compromise between two objective functions:
the Kling and Gupta Efﬁciency criteria (KGE; Gupta et al.
2009) and the Nash-Sutcliffe efﬁciency criterion calculated
on log-transformed ﬂows (NSE-LOG; Oudin et al. 2006).
These objective functions were selected for their combined
effectiveness in favoring both high and low ﬂows, and were
calculated using the R package hydroGOF (R Core Team
2020; Zambrano-Bigiarini 2020). To better interpret and
qualify the calibration performance, the percent-bias (Yapo
et al. 1996) and the root mean square error (RMSE; Singh
et al. 2005) were calculated as additional performance
metrics (Table 1, Fig. S2). Further details on the calibration
procedure can be found in Blanchette et al. (2022).
